title: Vectors in flat spacetime
part: I: Geometry and mechanics in flat spacetime
one_line_summary: Recasts special relativity in 4-vector language: vectors as coordinate-free arrows with basis expansions, Lorentz transformation of up- and down-indexed components, the Minkowski metric and invariant scalar products, a catalogue of physical 4-vectors (velocity, momentum, force, acceleration, current) with uniform acceleration as a showpiece, and finally the relativistic free-particle action -m times proper time, which hints that gravity will enter through the metric.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part I. Chapter 1 set up events, intervals, light cones and proper time; this chapter supplies the component and index machinery (Einstein summation, primes on indices, eta_{mu nu}, the rule that up-indices transform like differentials and down-indices like gradients) that Chapters 3-5 generalize to arbitrary coordinates, 1-forms, tensors and general metrics. Its closing action principle S = -m int dtau is the seed of the geodesic-from-action treatment in Chapters 8-9, and the weak-potential guess ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + ... foreshadows the metric of Chapter 5 and the Newtonian limit of Chapter 14.

assumed_background.topic: Events, intervals ds^2, light cones, proper time and dt/dtau = gamma
Twin paradox argument that the straight world line has the longest proper time
Calculus of variations and the Euler-Lagrange equation
Idea of covariance: laws that keep their form under a change of frame
3-vectors, Cartesian basis, dot product, Kronecker delta
Total differential and chain rule for partial derivatives
Hyperbolic functions sinh, cosh, tanh and simple linear ODEs
Newton's laws, kinetic and potential energy, power F.v
Lagrangian mechanics L = T - V (helpful but re-derived briefly)
Relativistic energy E = gamma m and momentum gamma m v
Continuity equation for a charge or particle density (used in Exercise 2.3)

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a vector is a geometric object (an arrow between two events) whose components depend on a chosen basis while the object itself does not.
Reader can expand a 4-vector as X = X^mu e_mu using the Einstein summation convention and correctly place indices upstairs for components and downstairs for basis vectors.
Reader can write down the boost matrix Lambda^{mu'}_nu for motion along x and identify it with the partial derivatives dx^{mu'}/dx^nu.
Reader can compute the Minkowski scalar product eta_{mu nu} X^mu Y^nu in the (-,+,+,+) signature and classify a vector as timelike, null or spacelike.
Reader can derive the condition eta_{mu' nu'} Lambda^{mu'}_mu Lambda^{nu'}_nu = eta_{mu nu} from invariance of the squared length and use it to show all scalar products are invariant.
Reader can show that basis vectors and gradient components transform with the inverse matrix, and state why the labels contravariant/covariant are avoided in favour of up/down.
Reader can explain why dx/dt fails to be a 4-vector and construct the 4-velocity u = dx/dtau with components (gamma, gamma v) and u.u = -1.
Reader can use the observer trick X^0_obs = -X.u (for example E = -p.u) and the result u.v = -gamma for two observers.
Reader can derive that 4-force and 4-acceleration are orthogonal to 4-velocity, relate f^mu to the 3-force, and interpret a.a as squared proper acceleration.
Reader can solve the uniform-proper-acceleration problem to obtain the hyperbolic world line x^2 - t^2 = 1/g^2 with v = tanh(g tau).
Reader can interpret the particle-current 4-vector J = n_0 u, including the gamma-enhanced density from length contraction.
Reader can state Hamilton's principle, apply the Euler-Lagrange equations to simple Newtonian Lagrangians, and show that L = -m/gamma reduces to the free Newtonian Lagrangian plus a constant.
Reader can explain how adding a weak potential to the relativistic action suggests a modified time-time metric component and why the action with g_{mu nu} is the natural GR generalization.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, chatty tour that treats special relativity as geometry in flat spacetime. The authors begin with the picture of a vector as an arrow between events, then immediately impose bases and coordinates so that index gymnastics can be practised in the easiest possible setting before curvature arrives. Much of the formal content is parked inside grey Example boxes and margin notes, leaving a main line that runs: arrows -> components -> transformation rules -> invariant dot product -> a table of physical 4-vectors each with its invariant -> the action principle. Every new vector is justified by checking its self-scalar-product, and 'compute in the easiest frame, then trust the invariant everywhere' is used repeatedly. The chapter ends by pointing forward: replace eta by g in the action and gravity becomes geometry.
narrative_arc: Classify quantities in flat spacetime: scalars (invariant numbers) versus vectors (arrows); note that flat spacetime allows one global coordinate system, unlike a curved Earth map.
Record events in coordinates x^mu = (ct, x) and set c = 1; insist a vector is defined by its transformation behaviour, not by being a list of numbers.
Define a vector as the arrow from event A to event B, then introduce basis vectors and the expansion X = X^mu e_mu by analogy with Euclidean 3-vectors.

Express the same arrow in two frames, write the Lorentz transformation of components in index and matrix form, and identify Lambda with partial derivatives of new coordinates with respect to old ones.
Build the scalar product from e_mu . e_nu, name it the Minkowski metric, tie its minus sign to ds^2, and classify vectors by their squared length using the light cone.
Demand invariance of length to get the defining identity of Lorentz matrices, then extend invariance to all scalar products.
Hold X fixed while changing frames to deduce that basis vectors (and gradients, and any down-indexed object) transform with the inverse matrix; summarize the up/down rules.
Tour the physical 4-vectors in Table 2.1, each with its invariant: position, velocity (after showing dx/dt fails), momentum (including photons), force, acceleration, particle current.
Showcase the machinery: observer-measured components as -X.u, relative gamma from u.v, 4-force orthogonal to 4-velocity, and the uniformly accelerated hyperbolic world line.
Switch to Lagrangian mechanics: action, Hamilton's principle, Euler-Lagrange equations checked on Newtonian examples.
Propose the relativistic action -m times proper time, check its low-velocity limit, add a weak potential to get a first hint of a gravitationally modified metric, and replace eta by g to preview GR.
signature_moves: Primes are put on indices (X^{mu'}, e_{mu'}) rather than on symbols, so that the index itself records which frame an object belongs to.
Upstairs-index objects are said to transform 'like differentials' and downstairs ones 'like derivatives', giving a calculus mnemonic instead of the words contravariant and covariant.
Each 4-vector is admitted only after its invariant self-product is computed; failure of dx/dt to give a frame-independent square is used as the proof it is not a 4-vector.
Evaluate a dot product in the frame where it is trivial (observer at rest, u = (1,0,0,0)) and export the result to all frames.
Decomposing another observer's 4-velocity as v/gamma = u + v_rel, with v_rel lying in U's spatial slice, to extract gamma = -u.v geometrically.
Humorous counterexample (the 'shopping vector' of fish and bread prices) to make the transformation criterion for vectors memorable.
Using the action principle as a bridge: a Newtonian check of L = -m/gamma followed by a potential-inserted version that reads off a metric, foreshadowing that gravity lives in g_{mu nu}.
Margin warnings that flag which flat-space habits will break in curved spacetime (the position vector, the vector-interval identification).

sections.title: Chapter opening: scalars, vectors and events in coordinates
sections.summary: After a Hamlet epigraph, the chapter distinguishes scalars (numbers agreed on by all inertial observers, such as charge and rest mass) from vectors (arrows in spacetime that can also be described by components in a basis). It notes that flat spacetime admits a single coordinate system valid everywhere, contrasting this with a city map that cannot cover a spherical Earth. Example 2.1 recaps events and observers and writes event coordinates as x^mu = (ct, x, y, z). On the following page units with c = 1 are adopted and the conventions of Greek indices for 4-vector components, Roman indices for spatial components, and bold italic symbols for 4-vectors are fixed, with the shopping-vector footnote warning that a vector must transform properly.
key_moves: Scalar defined by frame-independence; vector introduced geometrically.
Global coordinates are possible only because spacetime is flat; curved spacetime will need local patches.
Coordinates x^mu = (ct, x) with upstairs index; components depend on the basis.
A vector is defined by how its components transform, illustrated by the fish-and-bread counterexample.

sections.title: Vectors
sections.summary: A vector is defined as the difference B - A between two events, an object that needs no coordinates. To describe it numerically a set of basis vectors e_mu is introduced. Example 2.2 reviews Euclidean 3-vectors: components carry upper indices, basis vectors lower ones, Cartesian bases are orthonormal, and dotting with a basis vector projects out a component. By analogy a 4-vector is expanded as X = X^mu e_mu with the Einstein summation convention over repeated up-down index pairs. Margin notes explain that the index on e_mu labels which basis vector rather than a component, define the Kronecker delta, and warn that the close resemblance of vectors and intervals will not survive in curved spacetime.
key_moves: X = B - A makes the vector frame-free.
Euclidean warm-up fixes up/down index placement and projection by dot products.
X = X^mu e_mu with implicit summation.

sections.title: Coordinate transformations
sections.summary: The same vector is written in an unprimed and a primed basis, with primes attached to indices. Components transform between inertial frames with the Lorentz matrix Lambda^{mu'}_nu; Example 2.3 displays the standard boost along x. Treating the displacement dx as the archetypal vector and using the chain rule for differentials identifies Lambda^{mu'}_nu with dx^{mu'}/dx^nu, so components are said to transform like differentials. The scalar product is built from e_mu . e_nu, which in flat spacetime is the Minkowski metric diag(-1,1,1,1); its sign is chosen so that ds^2 = dx . dx. Vectors are classified as spacelike, null or timelike by the sign of X.X and placed relative to the light cone. Example 2.4 derives the Lorentz condition on Lambda from length invariance and generalizes to all scalar products. Example 2.5 keeps X fixed to show basis vectors transform with the inverse matrix, and Example 2.6 shows down-indexed objects such as gradients transform like derivatives. A boxed summary lists the three rules, and margin notes discuss metric signature, the origin of the words contravariant and covariant, and the d'Alembertian.
key_moves: X = X^mu e_mu = X^{sigma'} e_{sigma'}: same arrow, two bases.
Chain rule dx^{mu'} = (dx^{mu'}/dx^nu) dx^nu identifies Lambda with a Jacobian.
eta_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu gives X.Y = -X^0Y^0 + X^iY^i and ds^2 = eta dx dx.
Sign of X.X classifies vectors; light cone as an absolute separator.
Invariance of X.X for all X forces eta_{mu' nu'} Lambda Lambda = eta_{mu nu}.
Coordinate independence of X forces e_{alpha'} = Lambda^mu_{alpha'} e_mu with the inverse matrix.
Down-indexed objects (basis vectors, gradients) transform like partial derivatives with dx^nu/dx^{mu'}.

sections.title: Examples of vectors
sections.summary: Table 2.1 lists common 4-vectors with their invariants. The position vector works in special relativity but is flagged as the one that will not generalize. Velocity is first attempted as dx/dt, which fails because its square -1/gamma^2 depends on frame; differentiating by proper time instead gives u = (gamma, gamma v) with u.u = -1, tangent to the world line. Example 2.7 shows u = (1,0,0,0) in the rest frame, that any vector's time component measured by an observer is -X.u, and that two observers satisfy u.v = -gamma via the decomposition v/gamma = u + v_rel. Momentum p = m u has components (E, p) and invariant -m^2; Example 2.8 writes p = E v so the form extends to photons. Force f = dp/dtau is orthogonal to u; Example 2.9 relates f^mu to the Newtonian 3-force and recovers power F.v. Acceleration a = du/dtau is orthogonal to u and its square is the proper acceleration squared; Example 2.10 solves constant proper acceleration to find a hyperbolic world line. Finally particle current J = n_0 u gives density gamma n_0 via length contraction and flux as spatial components.
key_moves: dx/dt . dx/dt = -1/gamma^2 is frame dependent, so dx/dt is not a 4-vector.
u = dx/dtau = (gamma, gamma v), u.u = -1.
Evaluate X.u in the observer's rest frame to get X^0_obs = -X.u.
v/gamma = u + v_rel with u . v_rel = 0 yields gamma = -u.v.
p^mu = (E, E v) extends to massless particles.
Differentiate u.u = -1 to get u . du/dtau = 0, so f.u = 0 and a.u = 0.
f^0 = F.v gamma links the time component of 4-force to power.
Constant a.a = g^2 with a.u = 0 gives du^0/dtau = g u^1, du^1/dtau = g u^0, so t = sinh(g tau)/g, x = cosh(g tau)/g.
J^0 = gamma n_0 = n and J^x = n v^x as a flux.

sections.title: Principle of least action
sections.summary: The Lagrangian formulation is recalled: the action is the time integral of L = T - V along a path with fixed endpoints, and Hamilton's principle selects the path that makes it stationary, which the calculus of variations turns into the Euler-Lagrange equations. Example 2.11 checks this on a free particle (law of inertia), a general potential (Newton's second law), a harmonic oscillator and Newtonian gravity. Linking to Fermat's principle, the relativistic free-particle action is taken as -m times the elapsed proper time, the minus sign making stationary action correspond to maximal proper time. Since dtau = dt/gamma the Lagrangian is -m/gamma; Example 2.12 writes the action with eta_{mu nu} and the low-speed expansion recovers the Newtonian kinetic term plus a constant. Example 2.13 inserts a weak potential Phi and reads off ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 to leading order, a first hint that gravity alters the metric, with a caution that the spatial part is not yet trustworthy. The chapter closes by writing the GR action with g_{mu nu} in place of eta_{mu nu}, followed by the chapter summary.
key_moves: S = int L dt with L = T - V; endpoints fixed; stationary S gives Euler-Lagrange equations.
Newtonian examples verify the machinery before relativity.
S = -m int dtau: the minus sign turns 'longest proper time' into 'stationary minimum of S'.
L = -m/gamma = -m + m v^2/2 + ... reproduces free Newtonian motion.
Adding -m Phi to L and matching to -m sqrt(-ds^2) gives g_00 = -(1+2Phi).
Replace eta_{mu nu} by g_{mu nu} in the action: matter will act through the metric.

concepts.name: Lorentz scalar
concepts.definition: A single number whose value is the same for every inertial observer, for example electric charge, rest mass, or the scalar product of two 4-vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: First item in an inventory of what kinds of quantity can live in flat spacetime, before vectors are discussed.

concepts.name: event
concepts.definition: A point in spacetime, specified by a place and a time, such as the emission or reception of a photon; recorded by observers using the coordinate grid and local clocks.
concepts.how_introduced: Recapped from Chapter 1 in Example 2.1 as the basic currency of relativity, then assigned coordinates x^mu.

concepts.name: 4-vector
concepts.definition: A geometric arrow in spacetime, for instance the displacement from one event to another, whose four components in any inertial basis change by the Lorentz transformation when the frame changes while the arrow itself is unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined geometrically as B - A between two events, then contrasted with an arbitrary list of numbers via the shopping-vector counterexample, and finally expanded in a basis.
concepts.notes: Bold italic type marks 4-vectors. The paragraph just before Section 2.1 (not the chapter summary) names x^0 the timelike component and x^i the spacelike components that make up a 3-vector.

concepts.name: basis vectors
concepts.definition: A set of four reference vectors e_0,...,e_3 in terms of which any 4-vector is a linear combination; the lower index names which basis vector is meant, not a component.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed to turn the coordinate-free arrow into numbers; motivated by the Euclidean unit vectors e_x, e_y, e_z in Example 2.2.

concepts.name: vector components
concepts.definition: The coefficients X^mu that multiply the basis vectors in X = X^mu e_mu; they carry upper indices and depend on the chosen basis.
concepts.how_introduced: By analogy with a^x, a^y, a^z of a 3-vector, and extracted by projection with a dot product.

concepts.name: Einstein summation convention
concepts.definition: A repeated index that appears once upstairs and once downstairs in a term is summed over all its values (0 to 3 for Greek indices) without writing the sum sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced when writing X^mu e_mu, and a margin note writes out the explicit sum for Lambda^{mu'}_nu X^nu.

concepts.name: index conventions
concepts.definition: Greek indices run over 0-3 for spacetime components, Roman indices over 1-3 for spatial components; primes are placed on indices to denote the transformed frame, so X^{mu'} and X^mu are components of the same vector in different frames.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated before §2.1 and in a margin note at the start of §2.2, justified as paying off in complicated equations.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.definition: The symbol that equals 1 when its two indices are equal and 0 otherwise; the mixed version with one index up and one down represents the identity transformation.
concepts.how_introduced: First for orthonormal Euclidean bases, later in mixed form when composing a Lorentz matrix with its inverse.
concepts.notes: Why the mixed form needs one index up and one down is deferred to Chapter 4 (Exercise 4.2).

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: The linear map between the components of a 4-vector in two inertial frames that preserves the Minkowski scalar product; X^{mu'} = Lambda^{mu'}_nu X^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the empirical content of special relativity, written in matrix form for a boost in Example 2.3, then characterized by the invariance condition in Example 2.4.
concepts.notes: The chapter considers only origin-preserving transformations (no translations).

concepts.name: Lorentz boost matrix
concepts.definition: The 4x4 matrix with gamma on the t-t and x-x entries, -beta gamma on the t-x and x-t entries and 1 on the y and z diagonal, transforming components to a frame moving at speed beta along x.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.3 rewrites the Chapter 1 coordinate transformation as a matrix acting on a column of components.
concepts.notes: Its inverse is obtained by flipping the sign of beta (margin note 14).

concepts.name: Lorentz factor gamma
concepts.definition: gamma = (1 - v^2)^{-1/2} in units with c = 1; equals dt/dtau for a moving clock.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from Chapter 1 and used throughout the component formulas; re-derived geometrically from u.v in Example 2.7.

concepts.name: Jacobian of a coordinate change
concepts.definition: The transformation matrix of vector components equals the matrix of partial derivatives of the new coordinates with respect to the old: Lambda^{mu'}_nu = dx^{mu'}/dx^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: The displacement dx is a vector, and the chain rule for differentials transforms its components; comparing with the Lorentz rule identifies the matrices.
concepts.notes: A margin note stresses that this rule is what generalizes to arbitrary coordinates, whereas the position vector only follows it in special cases (Chapter 3).

concepts.name: Minkowski metric
concepts.definition: The matrix of scalar products of basis vectors in an inertial frame, eta_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1), which defines scalar products and the interval ds^2 = eta_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears when the dot product of two basis expansions is multiplied out, leaving a matrix of basis-vector products; its minus sign is fixed by consistency with the interval from Chapter 1.
concepts.notes: The inverse eta^{mu nu} is asserted to be the same matrix, with proof deferred to Chapter 4.

concepts.name: scalar product in spacetime
concepts.definition: The bilinear rule X.Y = eta_{mu nu} X^mu Y^nu = -X^0Y^0 + X^1Y^1 + X^2Y^2 + X^3Y^3, whose value is the same in all inertial frames.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by distributing (X^mu e_mu).(Y^nu e_nu) after a Euclidean warm-up.

concepts.name: metric signature
concepts.definition: The count or list of signs of the eigenvalues of the metric; the book uses (-,+,+,+), also written (3,1,0). Positive definite metrics are Riemannian; one sign differing from the rest is Lorentzian.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin jargon note beside the Minkowski matrix.
concepts.notes: The margin note lumps Lorentzian metrics under 'pseudo-Riemannian'; strictly pseudo-Riemannian covers any indefinite signature, with Lorentzian as a special case.

concepts.name: timelike, null and spacelike vectors
concepts.definition: With signature (-,+,+,+), a vector is timelike if X.X < 0, null if X.X = 0 and spacelike if X.X > 0; the classification is frame independent.
concepts.how_introduced: Extends the Chapter 1 classification of intervals to vectors, illustrated by arrows drawn relative to a light cone.

concepts.name: light cone
concepts.definition: The set of null directions through an event; timelike vectors from the event point inside the forward or backward cone, spacelike ones outside, null ones along it. Because it is Lorentz invariant it separates causal classes absolutely.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 1 with Fig. 2.4 labelling three arrows.

concepts.name: invariance of the scalar product
concepts.definition: Because Lorentz transformations preserve the length of every vector, their matrices satisfy eta_{mu' nu'} Lambda^{mu'}_mu Lambda^{nu'}_nu = eta_{mu nu}, and consequently every scalar product X.Y takes the same value in all inertial frames.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.4 substitutes the transformed components into the length and demands equality for all X, then extends to two different vectors.
concepts.notes: The step from invariance of X.X for all X to invariance of X.Y (polarization, using X+Y) is left to the reader.

concepts.name: transformation of basis vectors
concepts.definition: Since the vector X = X^mu e_mu is unchanged by a change of frame, the basis vectors must transform with the inverse of the component matrix: e_{alpha'} = Lambda^mu_{alpha'} e_mu.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.5 writes a general transformation for e_mu, substitutes both rules into X, and requires the product of matrices to be the identity.

concepts.name: inverse Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: The matrix Lambda^mu_{alpha'} = dx^mu/dx^{alpha'} that undoes Lambda^{alpha'}_mu, so that their contraction on the shared primed or unprimed index is a Kronecker delta; for a boost it is obtained by reversing the velocity.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified in Example 2.5 from the requirement that X be coordinate independent.

concepts.name: gradient as a down-indexed object
concepts.definition: The partial derivatives partial_mu phi = d phi/dx^mu of a scalar field, which transform with the inverse matrix, dx^nu/dx^{mu'}, like basis vectors; any object with a lower index is required to transform this way.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.6 applies the chain rule to derivative operators and notes that down-indexed quantities transform like derivatives, in contrast to up-indexed ones transforming like differentials.
concepts.notes: The book calls this a 'gradient vector' here; Chapter 4 recasts such objects as 1-forms.

concepts.name: contravariant and covariant components
concepts.definition: Traditional names for quantities that transform like coordinate differentials (upper index, contravariant) or like gradients (lower index, covariant).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only to be set aside; a margin note attributes the terms to Sylvester and explains that the authors reserve 'covariant' for 'transforms properly', preferring to say upstairs or downstairs.

concepts.name: d'Alembertian operator
concepts.definition: The Lorentz-invariant second-derivative operator partial^2 = eta^{mu nu} partial_mu partial_nu = -partial_t^2 + nabla^2, the spacetime analogue of the Laplacian.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing as useful for gravitational waves, with the component form in a margin note; practised in Exercise 2.3.

concepts.name: position 4-vector
concepts.definition: The arrow from the origin to an event with components (t, x); its self scalar product is -tau^2 for an event timelike-separated from the origin. It is a genuine vector under Lorentz transformations but not under general coordinate changes.
concepts.how_introduced: First row of Table 2.1 alongside the interval ds, with a boxed margin warning that it will not survive into GR while infinitesimal displacements will.
concepts.notes: Chapter 3 (§3.2) says farewell to it.

concepts.name: proper time
concepts.definition: Time elapsed on a clock carried along a world line; dtau^2 = -ds^2 for timelike displacements, and dt/dtau = gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from Chapter 1 and used as the frame-independent parameter needed to define 4-velocity, and later as the quantity whose total the relativistic action measures.

concepts.name: 4-velocity
concepts.definition: The derivative of a particle's spacetime position with respect to its proper time, u = dx/dtau, with components (gamma, gamma v); it is tangent to the world line and has u.u = -1 for any massive particle.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the failure of dx/dt, whose square -1/gamma^2 is frame dependent; replacing t by the invariant tau fixes the problem.
concepts.notes: For slow motion u^mu is approximately (1, v).

concepts.name: observer-measured components
aliases: projection onto an observer's time axis
concepts.definition: An observer with 4-velocity u measures the time component of any 4-vector X to be -X.u; for momentum this gives the energy they measure, E = -p.u.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.7(ii): evaluate the dot product in the observer's rest frame where u = (1,0,0,0), then invoke invariance. Repeated in the chapter summary and Exercise 2.1.
concepts.notes: The sign comes from eta_00 = -1; this is the seed of the Chapter 10 treatment of measurements.

concepts.name: relative velocity from u.v
concepts.definition: For two observers with 4-velocities u and v, the Lorentz factor of their relative motion is gamma = -u.v; in U's frame v/gamma = u + v_rel with v_rel lying in U's space.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.7(iii) decomposes v/gamma into a part along u and a spatial part orthogonal to u, drawn in Fig. 2.5, then dots with itself and with u.
concepts.notes: Exercise 2.2 turns this into a velocity-composition formula for gamma.

concepts.name: 4-momentum
concepts.definition: p = m u, with components (E, p) = (gamma m, gamma m v) and invariant p.p = -m^2; equivalently p^mu = (E, E v).
concepts.how_introduced: A short step from 4-velocity; Example 2.8 rewrites it using p = E v so that the formula can be applied to photons.

concepts.name: photon 4-momentum
concepts.definition: For a massless particle p^mu = (E, E v) with |v| = 1, a null vector with p.p = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted by extending the E-v form of the massive 4-momentum, since m u is meaningless when m = 0 and tau does not advance.
concepts.notes: The text calls the photon's velocity a null vector; strictly its 4-velocity cannot be defined via proper time, only its tangent direction.

concepts.name: 4-force
concepts.definition: f = dp/dtau = m du/dtau for constant rest mass; it is orthogonal to the 4-velocity and has components (gamma F.v, gamma F), where F = dp/dt is the 3-force.
concepts.how_introduced: Newton's second law rewritten in 4-vector language; differentiating u.u = -1 gives orthogonality, and Example 2.9 connects the time component to power.
concepts.notes: Newton's first law becomes du/dtau = 0.

concepts.name: normalization u.u = -1
concepts.definition: The 4-velocity of any massive particle has squared length -1 in every frame; differentiating it along the world line shows u . du/dtau = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed from (gamma, gamma v), confirmed in the rest frame, and then exploited to prove orthogonality of force and acceleration to velocity.

concepts.name: 4-acceleration
concepts.definition: a = du/dtau, orthogonal to u; in the instantaneous rest frame its time component vanishes and a.a equals the square of the proper acceleration.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed after force; a margin note rebuts the idea that special relativity cannot handle acceleration.

concepts.name: proper acceleration
concepts.definition: The acceleration measured in a body's instantaneous rest frame; its square equals the invariant a.a.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in a margin note beside the rest-frame evaluation of a.a.

concepts.name: instantaneous rest frame
concepts.definition: The inertial frame that at a given moment moves with the same velocity as an accelerating body; the body is at rest in it only instantaneously.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note explaining how inertial-frame special relativity can still describe accelerated motion.

concepts.name: uniformly accelerated (hyperbolic) motion
concepts.definition: Motion with constant proper acceleration g along x; with suitable initial conditions t = sinh(g tau)/g, x = cosh(g tau)/g, so the world line is the hyperbola x^2 - t^2 = 1/g^2 and the speed tanh(g tau) approaches but never reaches 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.10: the three invariant conditions u.u = -1, u.a = 0, a.a = g^2 reduce to coupled linear ODEs solved by hyperbolic functions; Fig. 2.6 sketches the curve.
formulas: t = g^{-1}\sinh g\tau,\ x = g^{-1}\cosh g\tau
concepts.notes: The book does not name Rindler; the name is ours.

concepts.name: particle current 4-vector
concepts.definition: For a cloud of particles with rest-frame number density n_0 and 4-velocity u, J = n_0 u; its time component is the density n = gamma n_0 seen in a given frame and its spatial components are particle fluxes.
concepts.how_introduced: Last entry in Table 2.1; the gamma in the density is explained by length contraction of a box of particles (Fig. 2.7).
concepts.notes: The printed component form uses u for the 3-velocity; see gaps. Chapter 12 builds the energy-momentum tensor from this idea.

concepts.name: length contraction
concepts.definition: A body moving at speed v is measured to be shorter by a factor gamma along its motion, so a fixed number of particles occupies a smaller volume.
concepts.how_introduced: Used from Chapter 1 to explain why the number density in a moving frame is gamma n_0.

concepts.name: action
concepts.definition: The integral of the Lagrangian along a trajectory between fixed initial and final configurations, S = int L dt; a number assigned to each possible path.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening of §2.4 as an alternative to Newton's laws, for a single particle in one dimension going from A to B.

concepts.name: Lagrangian
concepts.definition: A function of generalized positions, velocities and time characterizing a mechanical system; in Newtonian mechanics it is kinetic minus potential energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Attributed to Lagrange and worked out in several cases in Example 2.11.

concepts.name: Hamilton's principle of least action
concepts.definition: Among all paths with fixed endpoints, the physically realized one makes the action stationary (a minimum, maximum or saddle) under small variations.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the starting point replacing Newton's laws, with Fig. 2.8 showing a family of candidate paths sharing endpoints.
concepts.notes: Despite the name, the book notes the extremum need not be a minimum.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equations
aliases: equations of motion from the action
concepts.definition: The differential equations d/dt (dL/d qdot^i) = dL/dq^i, one per coordinate, satisfied by any path that makes the action stationary.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from the calculus of variations of Chapter 1 and immediately tested on Newtonian systems.
concepts.notes: Their geometric use (extremal paths) anticipates geodesics in Chapters 8-9.

concepts.name: calculus of variations
concepts.definition: The mathematics of finding functions (paths) that make an integral functional stationary, leading to the Euler-Lagrange equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Referenced back to Section 1.4 rather than re-derived.

concepts.name: law of inertia
concepts.definition: A body with no forces on it keeps a fixed speed and heading when viewed from an inertial frame; in 4-vector language its 4-velocity is constant, du/dtau = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Recovered from the free-particle Lagrangian in Example 2.11 and restated with 4-velocity.

concepts.name: Fermat's principle of least time
concepts.definition: Light travels between two points along a path for which the travel time is stationary (usually a minimum).
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as a cousin of Hamilton's principle to motivate an action proportional to elapsed proper time.
concepts.notes: The book says 'minimizes'; stationarity is the precise statement.

concepts.name: relativistic free-particle action
concepts.definition: The action for a free massive particle in special relativity is minus its rest mass times the proper time elapsed along its world line, S = -m int dtau = -m int (-eta_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu)^{1/2}, giving the Lagrangian L = -m/gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Fermat's principle and the twin-paradox result that straight world lines maximize proper time; the minus sign makes the extremum of S correspond to maximal tau; checked by the low-velocity limit in Example 2.12.
concepts.notes: Exercises 2.8 and 2.9 derive momentum gamma m v and energy gamma m from this Lagrangian.

concepts.name: non-relativistic limit
concepts.definition: Expanding relativistic expressions in powers of v (with c = 1) and keeping leading terms to check agreement with Newtonian physics.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to L = -m/gamma to recover m v^2/2 plus an irrelevant constant.

concepts.name: weak-field metric from a potential
aliases: first hint of gravity in the metric
concepts.definition: Adding the Newtonian potential energy -m Phi to the expanded free Lagrangian and interpreting the result as -m sqrt(-ds^2) suggests ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 to leading order, i.e. a gravitational potential modifies the time-time metric component.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.13 matches the Lagrangian with a potential to the proper-time form of the action, squares and drops small terms (shown in a margin derivation).
concepts.notes: A margin note warns that the spatial part also changes (see eqn 5.22); the correct weak-field metric has (1-2Phi) on the spatial terms.

concepts.name: metric tensor g_{mu nu}
concepts.definition: The position-dependent generalization of eta_{mu nu} that determines intervals in curved spacetime; in GR it is shaped by the distribution of mass-energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed at the end of the chapter by replacing eta_{mu nu} with g_{mu nu} in the proper-time action.
concepts.notes: Developed properly in Chapter 5.

concepts.name: geometrized units c = 1
concepts.definition: Time and length are measured in the same units so that the speed of light equals 1; then x^0 = t, beta = v, and E = gamma m.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced in bold at the top of printed p.23 and used for the rest of the book unless stated.
concepts.notes: Exercise 2.9 temporarily restores c.

concepts.name: spacetime coordinates
concepts.definition: Four numbers x^mu = (ct, x, y, z) labelling an event relative to an observer's grid and clocks; in flat spacetime one global inertial coordinate system suffices.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 2.1, with the contrast that curved spacetimes only allow local coordinates, like local maps of a spherical Earth.

key_equations.name: Event coordinates
key_equations.meaning: An event is labelled by one time and three space coordinates; the index is written upstairs.
key_equations.symbols: mu = 0..3; c speed of light (later set to 1)

key_equations.name: Vector as difference of events
key_equations.meaning: A vector in flat spacetime is the arrow from event A to event B, defined without coordinates.

key_equations.name: Euclidean basis expansion
key_equations.latex: \vec a = a^x\vec e_x + a^y\vec e_y + a^z\vec e_z
key_equations.meaning: A 3-vector is a combination of basis vectors with up-indexed components.

key_equations.name: Euclidean dot product
key_equations.latex: \vec a\cdot\vec b = a^x b^x + a^y b^y + a^z b^z
key_equations.meaning: Cartesian dot product in components.

key_equations.name: Orthonormal basis
key_equations.meaning: Cartesian basis vectors are unit length and mutually perpendicular.

key_equations.name: Projection of a component
key_equations.meaning: Dotting with a basis vector extracts the corresponding component (for an orthonormal Euclidean basis).

key_equations.name: 4-vector basis expansion
key_equations.meaning: Any 4-vector is its components times basis vectors, summed by the Einstein convention.

key_equations.name: Same vector in two bases
key_equations.meaning: The arrow is unchanged by a change of frame; only components and basis vectors change.
key_equations.symbols: primed indices refer to the primed frame

key_equations.name: Lorentz transformation of components
key_equations.meaning: Components of any 4-vector change between inertial frames by the Lorentz matrix; (2.11) repeats this after the explicit matrix.
key_equations.symbols: Lambda depends on relative velocity beta

key_equations.name: Boost along x in matrix form
key_equations.meaning: Explicit Lorentz matrix for frame S' moving at speed beta along x relative to S.

key_equations.name: Chain rule for differentials
key_equations.meaning: Ordinary calculus rule for how coordinate differentials transform.

key_equations.name: Lorentz matrix as Jacobian
key_equations.meaning: Vector components transform like coordinate differentials; this form generalizes beyond Lorentz transformations.

key_equations.name: Scalar product in a basis
key_equations.meaning: The dot product of two vectors is determined by the matrix of basis-vector dot products.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric
key_equations.meaning: Flat-spacetime metric in inertial coordinates with signature (-,+,+,+).

key_equations.name: Minkowski scalar product in components
key_equations.meaning: Rule for combining two 4-vectors into a scalar.

key_equations.name: Metric from basis vectors
key_equations.meaning: Metric components are the dot products of the basis vectors; boxed summary together with (2.18) and (2.19).

key_equations.name: Interval via the metric
key_equations.meaning: The squared interval is the self scalar product of the displacement vector; (2.18) restates X.Y = eta X Y.

key_equations.name: Causal classification of vectors
key_equations.meaning: The sign of the invariant squared length decides the causal character of a vector.

key_equations.name: Invariance of length
key_equations.meaning: The squared length computed in either frame agrees.

key_equations.name: Substituting transformed components
key_equations.meaning: Writing primed components in terms of unprimed ones inside the invariant.

key_equations.name: Defining condition for Lorentz matrices
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz transformations are exactly the linear maps that leave the Minkowski metric unchanged (matrix form Lambda^T eta Lambda = eta).

key_equations.name: Invariance of any scalar product
key_equations.meaning: All inner products of 4-vectors are frame independent.

key_equations.name: Basis vector transformation ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Primed basis vectors are combinations of unprimed ones with a matrix to be identified.

key_equations.name: Coordinate independence of X
key_equations.meaning: Requiring the arrow to be unchanged forces the two matrices to compose to the identity; (2.26) states X = X^mu e_mu = X^{alpha'} e_{alpha'}.

key_equations.name: Inverse Lorentz matrix
key_equations.meaning: Swapping which index is primed denotes the inverse transformation.

key_equations.name: Inverse identities
key_equations.meaning: Contracting a transformation with its inverse gives the mixed Kronecker delta in either frame.

key_equations.name: Transformation of derivative operators
key_equations.meaning: Down-indexed objects transform like partial derivatives, with old coordinates differentiated by new ones.
key_equations.symbols: y^{alpha'} denotes the primed coordinates (a one-off notation)

key_equations.name: Gradient transformation
key_equations.meaning: Components of the gradient of a scalar field transform with the inverse matrix.

key_equations.name: Rule for down-indexed components
key_equations.meaning: Any lower-index object transforms with the inverse of the component Lorentz matrix.

key_equations.name: d'Alembertian (margin note 16)
key_equations.meaning: Invariant wave operator, the spacetime version of the Laplacian.
key_equations.symbols: eta^{mu nu} numerically equal to eta_{mu nu}

key_equations.name: Position invariant
key_equations.meaning: Self scalar product of the position vector equals minus the squared proper time from the origin (for a timelike separation).

key_equations.name: dx/dt is not a 4-vector
key_equations.meaning: The would-be invariant depends on the frame's speed, so coordinate-time derivatives of position do not form a 4-vector.

key_equations.name: 4-velocity definition
key_equations.meaning: Differentiate position with respect to invariant proper time to get a genuine 4-vector tangent to the world line.

key_equations.name: 4-velocity components
key_equations.meaning: Components of the 4-velocity in terms of the ordinary 3-velocity; margin eqn (2.35) gives the slow limit (1, v).

key_equations.name: Normalization of 4-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Every massive particle's 4-velocity has squared length -1; used throughout the book.

key_equations.name: Observer-measured time component
key_equations.meaning: The time component of any vector as measured by an observer with 4-velocity u.

key_equations.name: Decomposition of another observer's velocity
key_equations.meaning: In U's frame, V's rescaled 4-velocity splits into U's time direction plus a purely spatial relative velocity orthogonal to u.

key_equations.name: Relative gamma
key_equations.meaning: Squaring the decomposition recovers the usual Lorentz factor of the relative speed.

key_equations.name: Scalar product of two 4-velocities
key_equations.meaning: The invariant dot product of two observers' 4-velocities gives minus their relative Lorentz factor.

key_equations.name: 4-momentum
key_equations.latex: p = mu,\quad p^{\mu} = (\gamma m, \gamma m\vec v) = (E, \vec p),\quad p\cdot p = -m^2
key_equations.meaning: Energy and momentum combine into one 4-vector whose invariant is the rest mass.

key_equations.name: Momentum-energy-velocity relation
key_equations.meaning: 3-momentum equals energy times velocity, valid also for massless particles.

key_equations.name: 4-momentum in E-v form
key_equations.meaning: Form of the 4-momentum that is adopted for photons.

key_equations.name: Relativistic Newton's second law
key_equations.meaning: 4-force is the proper-time rate of change of 4-momentum.

key_equations.name: Differentiating the normalization
key_equations.meaning: Because u.u is constant, 4-acceleration and 4-force are orthogonal to 4-velocity.

key_equations.name: Time component of 4-force
key_equations.meaning: From f.u = 0 with u = (gamma, gamma v). The printed intermediate line writes gamma f^0 - gamma f.v = 0, which has the overall sign flipped relative to the (-,+,+,+) product; the conclusion is unaffected.

key_equations.name: 4-force in coordinate-time rates
key_equations.meaning: Chain rule with dt/dtau = gamma, following the component form (2.47).

key_equations.name: 4-force in terms of 3-force
key_equations.meaning: Spatial part is gamma times the Newtonian 3-force F = dp/dt; time part is gamma times the power, consistent with dE/dt = F.v. (2.49) is the intermediate f^mu = (f^0, gamma F).

key_equations.name: Relativistic law of inertia
key_equations.meaning: A free particle's 4-velocity is constant; flat-space precursor of the geodesic equation.

key_equations.name: Acceleration orthogonal to velocity
key_equations.meaning: In the instantaneous rest frame the 4-acceleration has no time component.

key_equations.name: Invariant magnitude of acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Evaluated in the instantaneous rest frame, a.a is the squared proper acceleration.

key_equations.name: Constraints for uniform acceleration
key_equations.latex: u\cdot u = -1,\quad u\cdot a = 0,\quad a\cdot a = g^2
key_equations.meaning: Three invariant conditions that fix the motion with constant proper acceleration g; (2.54) gives the first-order definitions dt/dtau = u^0, dx^1/dtau = u^1, du^0/dtau = a^0, du^1/dtau = a^1.

key_equations.name: Coupled equations for uniform acceleration
key_equations.latex: a^0 = \frac{\mathrm{d}u^0}{\mathrm{d}\tau} = g u^1,\quad a^1 = \frac{\mathrm{d}u^1}{\mathrm{d}\tau} = g u^0
key_equations.meaning: Solving the constraints (margin note 23) gives linear ODEs whose solutions are hyperbolic functions.

key_equations.name: Hyperbolic world line
key_equations.latex: t = \frac{1}{g}\sinh g\tau,\quad x = \frac{1}{g}\cosh g\tau \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 - t^2 = g^{-2}
key_equations.meaning: A body with constant proper acceleration traces a hyperbola in the t-x plane.

key_equations.name: 4-velocity on the hyperbola
key_equations.meaning: Satisfies u.u = -1 automatically.

key_equations.name: 3-velocity under uniform acceleration
key_equations.meaning: Speed approaches but never exceeds 1.

key_equations.name: 4-acceleration on the hyperbola
key_equations.latex: a^0 = g\sinh g\tau,\quad a^1 = g\cosh g\tau,\quad |a| = \sqrt{-(a^0)^2 + (a^1)^2} = g
key_equations.meaning: The 4-acceleration components grow but its invariant magnitude stays g; the needed 4-force is m a^mu.

key_equations.name: Particle current
key_equations.latex: J = n_0 u,\quad J^{\mu} = \gamma n_0(1, \vec v),\quad n = \gamma n_0
key_equations.meaning: Density and flux of particles packaged as a 4-vector; printed with u in place of the 3-velocity v.

key_equations.name: Action
key_equations.meaning: Integral of the Lagrangian along a path between fixed endpoints.

key_equations.name: Newtonian Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic minus potential energy.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
key_equations.meaning: Condition for a path to extremize the action; (2.64) gives one such equation per coordinate x^i.

key_equations.name: Newton's second law from the Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equation for L = m xdot^2/2 - V(x); (2.65) is the free case giving xddot = 0.

key_equations.name: Newtonian gravity Lagrangian
key_equations.latex: L = \tfrac12 m(\dot x^2 + \dot y^2 + \dot z^2) + \frac{GMm}{|\vec r|}
key_equations.meaning: Kinetic energy minus gravitational potential energy -GMm/r. Printed with the square missing on xdot (confirmed on the page render); corrected here.
key_equations.symbols: G gravitational constant; M central mass

key_equations.name: Newtonian gravitational equations of motion
key_equations.meaning: Inverse-square attraction recovered from the Lagrangian.

key_equations.name: Relativistic free-particle action
key_equations.meaning: Action is minus rest mass times elapsed proper time; stationary action means maximal proper time.

key_equations.name: Relativistic free Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Follows from dtau = dt/gamma.

key_equations.name: Action in terms of the metric
key_equations.meaning: Makes explicit that the action is a length functional built from the metric.

key_equations.name: Low-velocity expansion of the Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Apart from an irrelevant constant, the Newtonian free Lagrangian is recovered.

key_equations.name: Proper time with a potential
key_equations.meaning: Matching L = -m + mv^2/2 - m Phi to -m sqrt(-ds^2)/dt.
key_equations.symbols: Phi Newtonian potential per unit mass

key_equations.name: Squaring and truncating
key_equations.meaning: Margin algebra; terms in Phi^2, v^2 Phi and v^4 are then dropped.

key_equations.name: Weak-potential line element
key_equations.meaning: First hint that a gravitational potential alters the metric; only the time part is reliable at this order (the spatial part is corrected in eqn 5.22).

key_equations.name: Free-fall action in curved spacetime
key_equations.meaning: In GR the flat metric is replaced by a metric shaped by gravitating matter; extremizing this gives geodesics.

key_equations.name: Relative gamma from two 3-velocities (Exercise 2.2)
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz factor of relative motion of two particles with lab velocities u and v.

key_equations.name: Lowered momentum components (Exercise 2.3)
key_equations.meaning: Index lowering flips the sign of the time component; (2.78) is p^mu = (E, p) and (2.80) the invariant.

key_equations.name: Gradient operator components (Exercise 2.3)
key_equations.meaning: Down-index derivative; raising gives partial^mu = (-partial_t, nabla). The exercise's part (iii) prints partial_mu J^mu = -d rho/dt + div J, but with these components the result is +d rho/dt + div J (the continuity-equation form).

figures.label: Fig. 2.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A rough attempt to draw 3+1-dimensional spacetime: the three space directions are squashed into a single shaded plane, with a time axis and a photon path added.
figures.visual_description: A vertical arrow labelled t rises from an origin. Three bold arrows labelled x (pointing left), y (down and to the right) and z (up and to the right) radiate from the same origin inside a stippled triangular plane viewed obliquely. A long dashed straight line labelled gamma passes through the origin from lower left to upper right, tilted between the time axis and the spatial plane.
figures.what_it_teaches: Spacetime has one time and three space directions that cannot all be drawn faithfully; diagrams compress space, and light follows a straight 45-degree-type path through the origin.

redesign.idea: A 3D spacetime viewer where the learner chooses which spatial dimension to suppress, turning a 3-space slice into a 2+1 diagram with a light cone and photon world line.
redesign.interaction: Toggle which of x, y, z is hidden; orbit the camera; drag a photon's direction and watch its world line stay on the cone.

figures.label: Fig. 2.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A vector exists without coordinates; imposing a basis lets it be written as components times basis vectors.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked sketches. Top: a straight arrow labelled X runs from a dot marked A at lower left to a dot marked B at upper right, with no axes. Bottom: the same arrow X drawn as the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose horizontal leg is an arrow labelled X^x e_x and whose vertical leg is an arrow labelled X^y e_y, meeting at the tip of X.
figures.what_it_teaches: Separates the geometric object (arrow between events) from its representation (component-weighted basis vectors).

redesign.idea: Fixed arrow between two draggable events with a rotatable, stretchable basis overlay; component readouts change while the arrow never moves.
redesign.interaction: Drag events A and B; rotate or skew the basis; see X^mu update and the reconstructed sum X^mu e_mu snap onto the same arrow.

figures.label: Fig. 2.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Unprimed and primed frames shown with a single space axis each.
figures.visual_description: An L-shaped pair of axes labelled t (vertical) and x (horizontal) with S near the corner. A second, smaller L-shaped pair labelled t' and x' sits displaced up and to the right, marked S', with a horizontal arrow labelled v pointing right from its vertical axis. A dot labelled P lies in the quadrant of the primed axes. Both frames are drawn with perpendicular axes (not as tilted Minkowski axes).
figures.what_it_teaches: The same event P can be described in two frames in relative motion; motivates primed indices for the second frame.

redesign.idea: Proper Minkowski diagram: S axes orthogonal, S' axes drawn as scissored lines determined by a velocity slider, with an event P whose coordinates are read off in both frames by grid lines parallel to each set of axes.
redesign.interaction: Slide beta from -0.9 to 0.9; drag P; readouts show (t,x) and (t',x') plus the matrix Lambda acting on the column vector, with -t^2 + x^2 displayed as unchanged.

figures.label: Fig. 2.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light cone and the three types of vector drawn from its apex.
figures.visual_description: An hourglass double cone with stippled elliptical rims top and bottom, apex in the middle. Three arrows leave the apex, all toward the upper right: the arrow labelled timelike climbs at a steep angle and stays inside the upper cone; the arrow labelled null runs along the upper cone's surface to its rim; the arrow labelled spacelike points only slightly above horizontal and exits the cones altogether.
figures.what_it_teaches: The sign of X.X corresponds to whether the arrow lies inside, on, or outside the light cone, and this classification is frame independent.

redesign.idea: Draggable arrow from the apex of a 2+1 light cone that colours itself by causal type and shows X.X live; a boost slider tilts components but never changes the colour.
redesign.interaction: Drag arrow tip in 3D; apply boosts; watch components change while X.X and classification stay fixed.

figures.label: Table 2.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Common 4-vectors with their self-scalar-product invariants; the position vector is flagged as not surviving general coordinate changes.
figures.visual_description: Three-column ruled table: physical quantity, 4-vector, invariant. Rows: interval ds with -dtau^2; position x with -tau^2 (asterisk); velocity u = dx/dtau with -1; momentum p = m u with -m^2; force f = dp/dtau with m^2|a|^2; acceleration a = du/dtau with |a|^2; current J = n_0 u with -n_0^2. Exported only as an HTML table, not an image.
figures.what_it_teaches: Every physical 4-vector comes with an invariant that all observers agree on; timelike ones have negative squares and the two derived by differentiating u are spacelike.

redesign.idea: Interactive 4-vector card deck: each card shows a world line with the vector drawn on it, components in the current frame, and its invariant.
redesign.interaction: Pick a particle speed and a frame velocity; all cards update components while the invariants column stays constant; clicking a card opens its derivation.

figures.label: Fig. 2.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: In observer U's frame, the rescaled 4-velocity v/gamma of a second observer splits into u plus a spatial relative velocity.
figures.visual_description: A shaded parallelogram drawn in perspective is labelled 'Spacelike three-space of U'. From a dot on it, a vertical arrow u points straight up, a longer diagonal arrow v/gamma points up and to the right, and a short horizontal arrow v_rel lies in the plane. Dotted lines complete a rectangle: one horizontal from the tip of u to the tip of v/gamma, one vertical from the tip of v_rel up to the tip of v/gamma.
figures.what_it_teaches: Vector addition v/gamma = u + v_rel with v_rel orthogonal to u; dotting with u isolates -gamma, and squaring gives gamma in terms of v_rel.

redesign.idea: Observer-split explorer: choose two world lines; the scene shows U's time axis and simultaneity plane, projects V's 4-velocity into parallel and orthogonal parts, and reports gamma = -u.v.
redesign.interaction: Drag V's velocity arrow; switch to V's frame to see the roles swap; toggle a Euclidean-looking versus Minkowski-correct drawing to highlight that 'orthogonal' uses eta.

figures.label: Fig. 2.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: A world line with constant proper acceleration is a hyperbola.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical) and x (horizontal). To the right of the t axis a curve touches the x axis at its closest point and bends away to larger x both above and below, like a sideways C opening to the right. Dots along the curve carry short tangent arrows pointing upward (future), one labelled u; the arrows tilt further from vertical the farther the point is from the x axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniform proper acceleration gives x^2 - t^2 = 1/g^2; the 4-velocity stays tangent and tilts toward but never reaches 45 degrees.

redesign.idea: Rocket with constant proper acceleration on a Minkowski diagram: world line, tangent u and orthogonal a arrows drawn with Minkowski orthogonality, plus the 45-degree asymptote.
redesign.interaction: Slider for g and for proper time tau; readouts of v = tanh(g tau), gamma, and |a| = g; a light pulse emitted from behind the asymptote never catches the rocket.

figures.label: Fig. 2.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A moving box is shorter along its motion, so the same particles are packed more densely.
figures.visual_description: Top: a long rectangular 3D box filled with scattered dots, with a double-headed arrow beneath labelled l. Bottom: a shorter box of the same height and depth, with dots that look more crowded, a double-headed arrow labelled l/gamma, and an arrow labelled v pointing right from its side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Why the time component of the particle current is gamma n_0: contraction reduces volume while particle number is fixed.

redesign.idea: Particle box whose length contracts as a speed slider increases, with a live count of particles per unit volume and a flux counter at a plane.
redesign.interaction: Slide v; see n = gamma n_0 and J^x = n v update; a Minkowski panel shows the corresponding J vector tilting.

figures.label: Fig. 2.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Several candidate paths connecting the same fixed start and end points.
figures.visual_description: Two dots: q(t1) at the left and q(t2) at the upper right. Five or six hand-drawn curves with arrowheads connect them, some wavy with wiggles, one arcing high above, and one making a wide loop below and around to the right; all share both endpoints.
figures.what_it_teaches: The action is evaluated on every path with the same endpoints and Hamilton's principle selects the extremal one; variations vanish at the ends.

redesign.idea: Action landscape explorer: the learner sketches or perturbs a path between fixed endpoints for a chosen Lagrangian (free, harmonic, uniform gravity, relativistic -m/gamma) and sees the action value; a gradient-descent button relaxes it to the true path.
redesign.interaction: Drag control points of a spline path; readout of S; toggle to a spacetime version where the relativistic action rewards the straight world line with maximal proper time.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.1
worked_examples.problem: Recap what an event is and how an observer assigns it coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Describe events as physical happenings recorded by observers with clocks and a coordinate grid; package the readings as x^mu = (ct, x, y, z) and view the event as an arrow from the origin.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinates of an event are frame-dependent labels; the event itself is not.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.2
worked_examples.method: Expand in basis vectors with up-indexed components, write the dot product, state orthonormality with the Kronecker delta, and project components out by dotting with basis vectors.
worked_examples.key_insight: The index placement rules and the projection trick are the same ones that will be adapted to spacetime, where the metric replaces delta_ij.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.3
worked_examples.problem: Write the Lorentz boost along x as a matrix acting on vector components.
worked_examples.method: Arrange the Chapter 1 transformation of (t, x, y, z) into a 4x4 matrix and abbreviate it with the summation convention.
worked_examples.key_insight: Transformation laws are matrix multiplication on component columns; index notation is shorthand for this.
worked_examples.result: Matrix (2.10) with gamma and -beta gamma entries.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.4
worked_examples.problem: Show what invariance of vector length implies for the Lorentz matrices and for general scalar products.
worked_examples.method: Write X.X in both frames, substitute the transformation of components, require equality for every X, and conclude eta_{mu' nu'} Lambda Lambda = eta_{mu nu}; then apply to X.Y.
worked_examples.key_insight: The metric is the thing Lorentz transformations preserve; this single identity is what makes dot products trustworthy across frames.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.5
worked_examples.problem: Determine how basis vectors transform given how components do.
worked_examples.method: Posit e_{alpha'} = Lambda^mu_{alpha'} e_mu, substitute both transformations into X = X^{alpha'} e_{alpha'}, and demand the result equal X^mu e_mu, so the matrices must multiply to the Kronecker delta.
worked_examples.key_insight: Components and basis vectors transform oppositely so that the arrow they build stays put.
worked_examples.result: Lambda^mu_{alpha'} is the inverse of Lambda^{alpha'}_mu; identities (2.29).

worked_examples.label: Example 2.6
worked_examples.problem: Find the transformation rule for lower-index objects such as the gradient of a scalar field.
worked_examples.method: Use the chain rule for partial derivative operators, with old coordinates differentiated by new ones, and apply it to d phi/dx^mu.
worked_examples.key_insight: Up indices transform like differentials dx^mu; down indices transform like derivatives d/dx^mu, i.e. with the inverse matrix.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.7
worked_examples.problem: Three uses of 4-velocity: its rest-frame form, extracting an observer's measured time component of any vector, and relating two observers' 4-velocities to their relative speed.
worked_examples.method: (i) In the rest frame u = (1,0,0,0) so u.u = -1. (ii) Compute X.u in that frame and invoke invariance. (iii) In U's frame write v/gamma = u + v_rel, dot with itself for gamma, dot with u for u.v.
worked_examples.key_insight: Work out a dot product in the frame where it is simplest; because it is invariant, the answer holds everywhere.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.8
worked_examples.problem: Express 4-momentum in a form that also applies to photons.
worked_examples.method: Use p = gamma m v and E = gamma m to get p = E v, then write p^mu = (E, E v).
worked_examples.key_insight: Eliminating m and gamma leaves a formula meaningful for massless particles, whose momentum vector is null.
worked_examples.result: p^mu = (E, E v^x, E v^y, E v^z).

worked_examples.label: Example 2.9
worked_examples.problem: Relate the components of the 4-force to the Newtonian 3-force.
worked_examples.method: Use f.u = 0 with u = (gamma, gamma v) to find f^0 = f.v; write f = dp/dtau with the chain rule dt/dtau = gamma to get f^mu = gamma(dp^0/dt, dp^i/dt); identify the spatial part with gamma F.
worked_examples.key_insight: The time component of the 4-force is essentially power, so energy conservation is built into the 4-vector law.
worked_examples.result: f^mu = (gamma F.v, gamma F), consistent with dE/dt = F.v.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.10
worked_examples.problem: Find the world line of a body with constant proper acceleration g along x.
worked_examples.method: Write first-order equations for t, x, u^0, u^1 in proper time; impose u.u = -1, u.a = 0, a.a = g^2 to get du^0/dtau = g u^1 and du^1/dtau = g u^0 (algebra in margin note 23); differentiate again to get simple exponential-type ODEs and pick initial conditions t = 0, x = 1/g at tau = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Invariant constraints turn an apparently hard accelerated-motion problem into coupled linear ODEs; the solution is a hyperbola, and special relativity handles acceleration perfectly well.
worked_examples.result: t = sinh(g tau)/g, x = cosh(g tau)/g, x^2 - t^2 = 1/g^2, v = tanh(g tau), a^mu = (g sinh g tau, g cosh g tau) with |a| = g.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.11
worked_examples.problem: Apply the Euler-Lagrange equations to simple Newtonian systems.
worked_examples.method: Insert L = T - V for a free particle in 1D and 3D, a particle in a potential V(x), a harmonic oscillator and a Newtonian point-mass potential, and compute the equations of motion.
worked_examples.key_insight: The single variational recipe reproduces the law of inertia, Newton's second law, simple harmonic motion and inverse-square gravity.
worked_examples.result: xddot = 0; m xddot = -dV/dx; m xddot = -k x; rddot = -GM r/r^3.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.12
worked_examples.problem: Write the relativistic free-particle action in terms of the metric components.
worked_examples.method: Substitute dtau = sqrt(-ds^2) and ds^2 = eta_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu into S = -m int dtau.
worked_examples.key_insight: The action is a metric-length functional, which is exactly what later allows eta to be swapped for g.

worked_examples.label: Example 2.13
worked_examples.problem: See what adding a Newtonian potential to the relativistic Lagrangian implies for the interval.
worked_examples.method: Add -m Phi to the expanded Lagrangian, equate L dt to -m sqrt(-ds^2), square, and discard terms of order Phi^2, v^2 Phi and v^4.
worked_examples.key_insight: A weak potential can be absorbed into the time-time component of the metric: gravity can be geometry.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -(1 + 2 Phi) dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 (time part only trustworthy).

worked_examples.problem: Test whether dx/dt qualifies as a 4-vector velocity.
worked_examples.method: Form its components (1, dx/dt), compute the Minkowski square and note it equals -1/gamma^2, which varies with frame; then differentiate with respect to tau instead and recompute.
worked_examples.key_insight: The self-scalar-product is a quick diagnostic: a real 4-vector must have a frame-independent square.
worked_examples.result: dx/dt fails; u = dx/dtau = (gamma, gamma v) with u.u = -1 succeeds.

worked_examples.problem: Check that L = -m/gamma is a sensible free-particle Lagrangian.
worked_examples.method: Expand sqrt(1 - v^2) for small v and drop the constant term, which does not affect the Euler-Lagrange equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: A relativistic proposal must reduce to Newtonian physics at low speed; constants in L are dynamically irrelevant.
worked_examples.result: L = -m + m v^2/2 + ..., so free Newtonian motion is recovered.

worked_examples.problem: Interpret the components of the particle current 4-vector for a moving cloud.
worked_examples.method: Write J = n_0 u in the rest frame as n_0(1,0,0,0) and in a general frame as gamma n_0(1, v); read the time component as density and spatial components as flux through planes.
worked_examples.key_insight: Density is not invariant; it grows by gamma because of length contraction, while n_0 is the invariant.
worked_examples.result: n = gamma n_0; J^x = n v^x particles per unit area per unit time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A local street map of New York cannot be extended to cover the whole spherical Earth
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why flat spacetime allows one global coordinate system while curved spacetime will only allow local coordinate patches.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The Earth's surface is curved space, not spacetime, and is visibly embedded in 3D; spacetime curvature is intrinsic with no outside view.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Try to lay a square grid over a globe versus a plane; distortion grows away from a chosen patch.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The 'shopping vector' of fish price and bread price
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A pair of numbers in brackets does not become a vector just by notation: rotating your trolley does not mix the prices, so the pair fails the transformation test.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Humorous and rotation-based rather than Lorentz-based; does not show what proper transformation looks like.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Rotate a coordinate grid under a genuine displacement arrow and under a 'price pair'; only the arrow's components mix consistently.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Up-indexed components behave like differentials dx, down-indexed ones like derivatives d/dx
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a calculus-based mnemonic for which matrix (Lambda or its inverse) acts, avoiding the confusing words contravariant and covariant.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Mnemonic only; the geometric distinction between vectors and 1-forms is left to Chapter 4.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Stretch the x axis by a factor k: displacement components shrink by 1/k while gradient components grow by k, shown side by side.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Twin paradox: the unaccelerated twin ages most
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Justifies the minus sign in S = -m int dtau: the physical straight world line maximizes proper time, so minimizing S corresponds to maximizing tau.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a reminder here; the maximality holds among timelike paths and is not proven in this chapter.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Drag a kink into a world line between two fixed events and watch the proper-time counter drop.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Fermat's principle: light takes the route of least time
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offers a familiar optical variational principle as a model for an action proportional to elapsed time along a path.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Fermat's time is stationary rather than always minimal, and photons have zero proper time, so the analogy is structural only.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Particles crowded into a contracted box
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Makes the gamma factor in the observed number density visual.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Ignores relativity of simultaneity in how 'the same particles' are counted.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Relativistic action as 'mass times path length in time'
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reads -m int dtau as an energy (m c^2) times a proper-time length, making it the spacetime analogue of a length functional whose extremals are straight lines.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The Minkowski 'length' of a timelike path is maximized, not minimized, by straight lines, opposite to Euclidean intuition.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Compare a Euclidean shortest-path demo with the Minkowski longest-proper-time demo on the same pair of points.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any list of numbers written in brackets is a vector.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A vector is defined by how its components change under coordinate transformations; arbitrary lists (like prices) do not transform properly.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Programming and school algebra call any ordered list a vector.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its square -1/gamma^2 is frame dependent, so it is not a 4-vector; the 4-velocity uses proper time, u = dx/dtau.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian velocity is dx/dt and coordinate time looks like the natural parameter.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Special relativity cannot describe accelerated motion; you need general relativity for that.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Special relativity handles acceleration using instantaneous rest frames and 4-acceleration; Example 2.10 solves uniform acceleration exactly.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: SR is introduced via inertial frames, and GR is often advertised as the theory of accelerated frames.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Covariant vector' means a vector that transforms properly and 'contravariant' means one that does not.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Both kinds transform properly; the labels only indicate lower versus upper index placement (gradient-like versus differential-like), which is why the book prefers 'upstairs/downstairs'.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: 'Covariant' is also used for 'form-invariant under transformations'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The position vector is as fundamental in general relativity as in special relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Position vectors from an origin only transform properly under linear (Lorentz) transformations; in GR only infinitesimal displacements dx^mu survive as vectors.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Euclidean and Minkowski space the position vector is the first vector anyone meets.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Vectors and intervals between events are the same thing.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They coincide in flat spacetime, but in curved spacetime vectors live at a point (tangent spaces) and finite separations are not vectors.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Eqn 2.2 defines a vector as B - A.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The principle of least action always picks the path of minimum action.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The physical path makes the action stationary: it can be a minimum, maximum or saddle.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A straight world line has the shortest proper time between two events, as a straight line is shortest in Euclidean space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Minkowski spacetime the straight timelike world line has the longest proper time; hence the minus sign in S = -m int dtau.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Euclidean geometry trains us that straight means shortest.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Perpendicular 4-vectors look perpendicular on a spacetime diagram.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Minkowski orthogonality u.a = 0 means the two arrows are mirror-symmetric about the light cone line, not at a Euclidean right angle, except in the rest frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Figures such as Fig. 2.5 draw u and v_rel at right angles, which is only accurate in U's own frame.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Eqn 2.75 is the correct weak-field metric of GR.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the time-time part is reliable at this order; the spatial part also picks up a factor (1 - 2 Phi), as shown later (eqn 5.22).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation looks complete and gives a tidy line element.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Number density is a Lorentz scalar.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the rest-frame density n_0 is invariant; the density measured by a moving observer is gamma n_0 and is the time component of J.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Counting particles per volume sounds frame independent.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Components with a minus sign in the time slot mean the metric makes time 'imaginary' or negative.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The minus sign in eta_00 simply encodes that timelike separations have negative squared interval in this signature; conventions with (+,-,-,-) flip all signs without changing physics.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Older texts used ict and learners see -t^2 as strange.

thought_experiments.name: Rotating the shopping trolley
thought_experiments.setup: Treat the prices of fish and bread as a two-component 'vector' and turn your trolley by 45 degrees at the checkout.
thought_experiments.lesson: The prices do not mix as components of a real vector would; being a vector means transforming correctly.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Side-by-side rotation of a real displacement and a price pair, with component readouts.

thought_experiments.name: Constant-thrust rocket
thought_experiments.setup: A body experiences the same acceleration g in each of its momentary rest frames for all proper time.
thought_experiments.lesson: It follows a hyperbola approaching the light cone asymptotically, never reaching light speed, though its proper acceleration never changes.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated rocket on a Minkowski diagram with speedometer v = tanh(g tau) and onboard clock.

thought_experiments.name: Boxed particle cloud seen in motion
thought_experiments.setup: A box of particles at rest has density n_0; view it moving at speed v.
thought_experiments.lesson: Length contraction raises the observed density to gamma n_0, and the particles form a flux; density and flux unite in one 4-vector.

thought_experiments.name: Many trial paths with the same endpoints
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine every possible route a particle could take between q(t1) and q(t2) and assign each an action.
thought_experiments.lesson: Nature's route is the one whose action does not change to first order under small wiggles.

historical_notes.event: Coined the terms contravariant and covariant for the two transformation behaviours.
historical_notes.significance: The authors regard the terminology as unfortunate and replace it with upstairs/downstairs index language.

historical_notes.event: Lagrange (1736-1813 in the margin) showed that equations of motion can be obtained by making an integral over the path stationary, with the Lagrangian taken as kinetic minus potential energy.
historical_notes.significance: Provides the action-based route that the book uses to connect mechanics to spacetime geometry.

historical_notes.event: Principle that the realized motion makes the action stationary (name and dates given in the margin).
historical_notes.significance: Starting point for the relativistic proper-time action and later for geodesics.

historical_notes.event: Principle of least time for light rays (mentioned without biography).
historical_notes.significance: Used as the conceptual model for an action measuring elapsed time.

historical_notes.event: Instead of adding a gravitational potential to the Lagrangian, made matter shape the metric of spacetime itself.
historical_notes.significance: Motivates replacing eta_{mu nu} by g_{mu nu} in the action, the conceptual step from SR to GR.

applications_and_observations.details: Galaxy about 1e5 light years across; highest-energy cosmic rays around 1e19 eV; proton rest energy about 1 GeV. Our estimate: gamma is about 1e10, so the crossing takes about 1e5 years in the Galaxy frame and about 1e5 yr / 1e10 = 1e-5 yr, roughly 5 minutes, in the proton frame.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: gamma ~ 1e10; ~1e5 yr (Galaxy frame); ~3e2 s (proton frame, our estimate)

applications_and_observations.details: The time component of the 4-force reproduces the classical result that energy changes at the rate F.v.
