Using Example 2.10 with g = 9.8 m/s^2 (1/g is about 0.97 light-years in c = 1 units), after one year of proper time v = tanh(1.03) is about 0.77c; after five years v is about 0.9999c. These numbers are our own estimate, not the book's.

applications_and_observations.topic: Photon absorption by a free electron (Exercise 2.6)
applications_and_observations.details: 4-momentum conservation plus invariance of p.p forbids a free electron from absorbing a single photon, which is why absorption needs a nucleus or lattice to take up momentum.

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 from printed p.23 onward unless stated; x^0 = t, beta = v, E = gamma m.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Exercise 2.9 restores c in E = gamma m c^2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: eta_{mu nu} = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1), signature (-,+,+,+), so ds^2 = -dt^2 + dx^2 and timelike vectors have negative squares.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Margin note also calls it (3,1,0) and mentions the opposite (+,-,-,-) convention.

notation_and_conventions.convention: 4-vectors in bold italic (X, u, p); 3-vectors with an arrow over the symbol.
Greek indices 0-3 for spacetime; Roman indices 1-3 for space; components upstairs, basis vectors downstairs.
Frame change indicated by priming the index, e.g. X^{mu'}, e_{alpha'}, Lambda^{mu'}_nu; the position of the prime (upper or lower) tells which direction the matrix maps.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Eqn 2.30 briefly uses y^{alpha'} for primed coordinates.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Lambda^{mu'}_nu = dx^{mu'}/dx^nu acts on up components; Lambda^nu_{mu'} = dx^nu/dx^{mu'} is its inverse and acts on down-indexed objects and basis vectors.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Boost along x has -beta gamma off-diagonal entries.

notation_and_conventions.convention: X^2 means X.X, which can be negative, zero or positive; |a| denotes sqrt of a.a for a spacelike acceleration.
u^mu = (1, 0) abbreviates (1, 0, 0, 0) with a 3-vector in the second slot.
partial^2 = eta^{mu nu} partial_mu partial_nu = -partial_t^2 + nabla^2; eta^{mu nu} numerically equals eta_{mu nu}.
S = -m int dtau with the minus sign so the extremum is a minimum of S (maximum of tau).

margin_notes.summary: Index placement matters: coordinates carry upstairs indices, and whether an index is up or down will acquire meaning later.
Coordinates of an event are frame-dependent labels: a different basis gives different numbers for the same event.
The shopping-vector counterexample: prices of fish and bread do not transform when the trolley is rotated, so they are not a vector; vectors must transform covariantly (pointer back to page 3).
Vectors and intervals look alike in flat spacetime, but the resemblance breaks down in curved spacetime.
The index on e_mu tells which basis vector, not which component.
Definition of the Kronecker delta delta_ij (1 when the indices match, 0 otherwise), used for the orthonormal Cartesian basis.
Primes sit on indices, not symbols, to mark the transformed frame; this pays off in complicated equations.
Summation written out explicitly; all transformations considered keep the origin fixed.
Only Lorentz transformations are used in this chapter, but the Jacobian rule will apply to vector components generally; the position vector obeys it only in special cases (next chapter).
Jargon on signature: eigenvalue signs of the metric; positive definite is Riemannian, one sign different is Lorentzian, described as pseudo-Riemannian.
The mixed Kronecker delta with one index up and one down is needed for reasons explained after tensors are introduced (Chapter 4, Exercise 4.2).
Check the inverse matrix by flipping the sign of beta in the boost.
Factors in index expressions are just numbers, so their order can be rearranged freely (used in eqn 2.27).
Contravariant/covariant terms trace to Sylvester; since both types transform properly, the book says upstairs/downstairs instead.
Component form of the d'Alembertian; eta^{mu nu} shown to equal eta_{mu nu} as a matrix in Chapter 4.
Boxed aside: the position vector will not upgrade to GR, though infinitesimal displacements and the other listed vectors will.
Boxed 'velocity component trick': spatial 4-velocity components equal the ordinary velocity times u^0.
Slow-motion limit u^mu approx (1, v); massive particles have timelike velocity with negative square.
Lorentz covariant here simply means the object transforms correctly under Lorentz transformations.
Spacelike 3-space of an observer means the purely spatial directions in their frame; eqn 2.39 can be checked by components.
Special relativity can treat acceleration through a sequence of instantaneous rest frames.
Proper acceleration defined as the rest-frame acceleration, whose square is a.a.
Algebra solving the three invariant conditions for a^0 and a^1 and choosing hyperbolic solutions with t = 0 at tau = 0.
Names and dates of Lagrange (1736-1813) and Hamilton (1805-1865) in the margin; portraits appear not to be printed in this copy.
The Lagrangian written with scalar q_i assumes 1D motion per particle; in 3D the arguments become 3-vector positions and velocities.
Squaring-and-truncation algebra leading to the weak-potential metric, dropping Phi^2, v^2 Phi and v^4 terms.
Caution that the low-speed derivation only constrains the time part; spatial coordinates need correcting too (eqn 5.22).
One-line check that L = -m/gamma integrated over coordinate time gives back S = -m times total proper time.

skills_practiced: manipulating u.v = -gamma into a composition formula
lowering indices with eta and computing invariants p_mu p^mu
raising the gradient index and forming the d'Alembertian and a 4-divergence
order-of-magnitude time dilation with ultra-relativistic gamma
applying a Lorentz boost to a rest-frame 4-momentum and checking invariance
deriving canonical momentum and Hamiltonian from L = -m/gamma

notable.summary: Prove that an observer with 4-velocity u assigns energy -p.u to a particle of 4-momentum p.
notable.why_notable: Turns the chapter's key observer trick into the formula used throughout GR for measured energies and redshifts.

notable.summary: Starting from u.v = -gamma, express the relative Lorentz factor in terms of two lab-frame 3-velocities, take the slow limit, and interpret the result.
notable.why_notable: Shows how an invariant statement yields velocity addition without any boost matrices.

notable.summary: Lower the index on the momentum 4-vector, verify the mass-shell invariant, raise the gradient's index, and build the d'Alembertian, the 4-divergence of a current, and the contraction of acceleration with velocity.
notable.why_notable: First hands-on index gymnastics with eta before Chapter 4 formalizes 1-forms; note that part (iii) as printed has a sign error on the time-derivative term.

notable.summary: Estimate how long the most energetic cosmic-ray protons take to cross the Galaxy in the Galaxy frame and in their own frame.
notable.why_notable: Dramatic numbers (gamma of order 1e10, minutes versus 1e5 years) make time dilation vivid.

notable.summary: Use 4-momentum conservation to prove a free electron cannot absorb one photon.
notable.why_notable: Classic demonstration that squaring 4-vector conservation laws beats component bookkeeping.

notable.summary: Find the shape of a hanging string by the action principle.
notable.why_notable: Needs a constraint (fixed length) and is a non-dynamical variational problem, stretching the Lagrangian idea beyond particle motion; the answer is a catenary.

notable.summary: Show that the relativistic Lagrangian -m/gamma gives canonical momentum gamma m v.
notable.why_notable: Confirms the action proposal reproduces relativistic momentum, not just the Newtonian limit.

notable.summary: Construct the Hamiltonian from L = -m/gamma and show it equals the relativistic energy.
notable.why_notable: Closes the loop from action to energy gamma m c^2.

difficulty.notes: The physics is standard special relativity, but the chapter front-loads index machinery: primed indices, Lambda versus its inverse distinguished only by prime position, eta^{mu nu} and lowered indices used before they are defined, and dense Example boxes. Example 2.10 and the weak-potential derivation in Example 2.13 require careful algebra. Conceptually gentle otherwise, with helpful mnemonics, but several printed slips (eqn 2.67, Example 2.9, Exercise 2.3(iii), u used for 3-velocity in the particle current) can trip careful readers.

cross_references.reason: Discussion of covariance (printed p.3) that the shopping-vector note appeals to.
Intervals, light cones and the Lorentz transformation reused in index form.
Calculus of variations, dt/dtau = gamma and the twin-paradox result that straight world lines maximize proper time.
Why the position vector fails under general coordinate transformations.
Proof that eta^{mu nu} is the same matrix as eta_{mu nu}; down-indexed objects recast as 1-forms.
Why the Kronecker delta used as identity must carry one index up and one down.
Eqn 5.22 corrects the spatial part of the weak-potential metric guessed in eqn 2.75.
Gravitational time dilation, the physical meaning of g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi).
Extremal intervals: the proper-time action becomes the route to geodesics.
Geodesic equation derived from the action with a general metric, eqn 2.76.
Observers and measurement generalize the -X.u rule.
Particle current and dust lead to the energy-momentum tensor.
The d'Alembertian is flagged as the operator of gravitational-wave theory.

teaching_gems.gem: Admit a candidate 4-vector only if its self-scalar-product is frame independent: dx/dt fails with -1/gamma^2, dx/dtau passes with -1.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a one-line diagnostic instead of an abstract transformation criterion, and explains why proper time must appear.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Vector audition panel: learner proposes a component recipe (dx/dt, dx/dtau, E and p, price pair), boosts it, and a meter shows whether its square stays fixed.

teaching_gems.gem: Compute any invariant in the frame where it is trivial, then trust it in every frame (X^0_obs = -X.u; u.v = -gamma).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces messy boosts with a strategy that recurs across all of GR (measured energies, redshifts).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Split-screen: same two vectors shown in lab frame and observer frame; the dot product readout is identical while components differ; a 'switch to easy frame' button animates the boost.

teaching_gems.gem: Up indices transform like differentials, down indices like derivatives.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Anchors an abstract transformation law in the chain rule every learner knows and sets up 1-forms.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stretch or boost coordinates under a fixed displacement arrow and a fixed gradient field; show the two component sets responding with Lambda and its inverse.

teaching_gems.gem: Keep the arrow fixed to deduce how the basis must change: components and basis vectors transform inversely so their product is unchanged.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the inverse-matrix rule a consequence of geometry rather than a rule to memorize.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Fig. 2.2 redesign with a boost slider showing basis arrows scissoring while components compensate.

teaching_gems.gem: Decompose another observer's 4-velocity as v/gamma = u + v_rel to read off gamma = -u.v.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A picture of vector addition yields a relativistic formula with no boost algebra and introduces the observer's spatial slice.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Fig. 2.5 redesign: drag V's velocity and watch the projection and gamma update.

teaching_gems.gem: Differentiate u.u = -1 to learn that force and acceleration are always orthogonal to velocity, then use invariants alone to solve constant proper acceleration.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows the power of constraints over brute-force components and yields the memorable hyperbola.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Hyperbolic rocket animation with u and a arrows drawn Minkowski-orthogonal and the invariant |a| = g held fixed.

teaching_gems.gem: Action = -m times proper time, checked by the Newtonian limit, then a potential inserted to read off a modified g_00, then eta replaced by g.
teaching_gems.why_effective: In one page it links Lagrangian mechanics, the twin paradox and the idea that gravity lives in the metric, motivating the whole book.
teaching_gems.app_idea: World-line relaxer: drag a path between two events in a potential well; the app computes the proper-time action with g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi) and relaxes to the free-fall path, which matches the Newtonian parabola.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 2.67 prints the kinetic term with xdot instead of xdot squared (confirmed on the page render).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader applying Euler-Lagrange gets an inconsistent x-equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the corrected Lagrangian and note the potential energy is -GMm/r, giving +GMm/r in L.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 2.9 writes (f^0, f).(gamma, gamma v) = gamma f^0 - gamma f.v, the negative of the (-,+,+,+) scalar product.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners checking signs may doubt the metric convention; the conclusion f^0 = f.v is unaffected.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 2.3(iii) states partial_mu J^mu = -d rho/dt + div J, but with partial_mu = (d/dt, nabla) the correct result is +d rho/dt + div J.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who compute correctly will think they erred; the continuity equation's sign matters later for conservation laws.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Flag the sign and connect partial_mu J^mu = 0 to the continuity equation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The particle-current paragraph uses u both for the 4-velocity and for the particles' 3-velocity (J^mu = gamma n_0 (1, u), J^x = gamma n_0 u^x).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses 4-vector and 3-vector symbols right after the chapter insisted on distinguishing them.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use v for the 3-velocity: J^mu = gamma n_0 (1, v).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 2.3 draws the primed frame's axes perpendicular and simply displaced, not as tilted Minkowski axes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Novices may think a boosted frame is just a shifted Cartesian grid, missing relativity of simultaneity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair it with a proper Minkowski diagram whose primed axes tilt symmetrically toward the light line.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The step from invariance of X.X for all X to invariance of X.Y is asserted but not shown.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may not see why a condition on lengths constrains all dot products.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the polarization trick: expand (X+Y).(X+Y) in both frames.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: eta^{mu nu} and lowered indices (partial^2, p_mu in Exercise 2.3) are used before inverse metrics and index raising are defined.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Index gymnastics feel like unexplained rules.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Introduce eta^{mu nu} as the matrix inverse of eta_{mu nu} and show numerically that it equals diag(-1,1,1,1) before using it.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The photon's 'velocity' is called a null vector, but u = dx/dtau cannot be defined when dtau = 0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may try to normalize a photon 4-velocity or divide by zero proper time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say only the tangent direction is null; parametrize photon paths with an affine parameter (as later chapters do) and define p directly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Distinguishing Lambda^{mu'}_nu from its inverse Lambda^nu_{mu'} relies solely on where the prime sits.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Easy to multiply by the wrong matrix; OCR and handwriting lose primes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Always pair index notation with the explicit boost matrix and its beta -> -beta inverse, and practise with numbers.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 2.75 looks like a finished weak-field metric though only g_00 is justified; the caution lives in a margin note.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may later use a wrong spatial metric for light bending (getting half the deflection).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the full weak-field metric with (1 - 2 Phi) spatial factor as a preview and explain why slow particles only probe g_00.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Table 2.1's force invariant m^2|a|^2 assumes constant rest mass and uses |a| for proper acceleration without saying so in the table.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Annotate the table: |a| is the rest-frame acceleration, f = m a holds for constant m.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Minkowski orthogonality never gets a picture. Fig. 2.5 is explicitly drawn in U's own frame, where u and v_rel really do look perpendicular, but the chapter never shows how the same orthogonal pair looks from any other frame.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who carry the right-angle picture into a boosted diagram get simultaneity slices and orthogonal 4-vectors wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show orthogonal pairs as mirror images across the 45-degree line in a general frame.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 2.8's caption uses the variation symbol delta q (vanishing at both endpoints), but the text never defines a variation; the Euler-Lagrange derivation is only referenced back to Section 1.4.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers who skipped Chapter 1's variational calculus meet delta q with no explanation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define a variation as q(t) + epsilon eta(t) with eta(t1) = eta(t2) = 0 and show one line of dS/d epsilon = 0.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Is a pair of numbers, like the prices of fish and bread, a vector? What would make it one?' Let the learner discover that transformation behaviour is the criterion.

Order of explanation that works: arrow between events -> basis and components -> boost matrix on components -> metric and dot product -> invariance -> inverse transformation for basis vectors -> physical 4-vectors -> action.
Before index notation, have the learner multiply the explicit boost matrix on (t, x) = (1, 0) and check that -t^2 + x^2 is unchanged; then reveal Lambda^T eta Lambda = eta as the general statement.
Check for understanding: ask why the minus sign sits in eta_00 and what X.X < 0 means geometrically on a light-cone picture.
When introducing 4-velocity, ask the learner to compute dx/dt . dx/dt first; the failure motivates proper time better than any statement.
Drill the observer trick: 'An observer moves with u; a particle has p. What energy does the observer measure?' Expect -p.u, and ask them to verify in the rest frame.
Common learner question: 'Why do basis vectors transform the opposite way?' Answer by holding the arrow fixed while shrinking the unit length: components must grow as basis vectors shrink.
Common learner question: 'Doesn't acceleration need GR?' Point to the hyperbolic rocket solution and the instantaneous rest frame idea; GR is about gravity, not acceleration per se.
For the action: ask which path between two events a free clock should take to record the most time, then connect the minus sign in S = -m int dtau to that maximum.
Warn about printed slips: eqn 2.67 missing square, Example 2.9 sign, Exercise 2.3(iii) sign, and u used for 3-velocity in the current; turn them into 'spot the error' checks for strong learners.
Flag clearly that eqn 2.75 is only half right and that the position vector will be abandoned in Chapter 3, so learners do not over-invest in either.

Adapt level: for novices keep c visible and use the explicit 2x2 boost; for advanced learners introduce rapidity (v = tanh of rapidity) to connect the hyperbola in Example 2.10 with boosts as hyperbolic rotations.
